'''New Paltz''' is a [[village]] in [[Ulster County, New York|Ulster County]] located in the [[U.S. state]] of [[New York (state)|New York]]. It is approximately {{convert|80|mi|km|-1}} north of [[New York City]] and {{convert|70|mi|km|-1}} south of [[Albany, New York|Albany]]. The population was 7,324 at the 2020 census.<ref name="2020Census">{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/newpaltzvillagenewyork,monroecountynewyork/PST045219|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=August 14, 2021|title=Quickfacts - New Paltz village, New York}}</ref>

New Paltz is located within the town of [[New Paltz (town), New York|New Paltz]], and is home to the [[State University of New York at New Paltz]], founded in 1828. The town is served by exit 18 on the [[New York State Thruway]], as well as state routes 299, 32, and 208; it is also about 90 minutes from both [[New York City]] and [[Albany, New York|Albany]].
== History ==
The [[Elting Memorial Library]], [[Guilford-Bower Farm House]], [[Jean Hasbrouck House]], [[Major Jacob Hasbrouck Jr. House]], [[Huguenot Street Historic District]], [[Mohonk Mountain House|Lake Mohonk Mountain House Complex]], [[New Paltz Downtown Historic District]], and [[The Locusts]] are listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]].<ref name="nris">{{NRISref|version=2010a}}</ref>
=== Early development ===
[[File:Beers Ulster County Atlas Page097.jpg|thumb|left|An 1875 map of the town of [[New Paltz (town), New York|New Paltz]]; the village was created in the central portion]]
New Paltz was founded in 1678 by French [[Huguenots]] settlers, including [[Louis DuBois (Huguenot)|Louis DuBois]], who had taken refuge in [[Mannheim]], Germany, for a brief period of time, being married there in 1655, before emigrating to the Dutch colony of [[New Netherland]] in 1660 with his family. Mannheim was a major town of the [[Palatinate (region)|Palatinate]] (in German, the ''Pfalz''), at the time a center of Protestantism. The settlers lived in [[Wiltwyck]] (present day [[Kingston, New York]]) and in 1677 purchased a patent for the land surrounding present day New Paltz from a [[Lenape]] tribe known as the [[Esopus tribe|Esopus]].

The people of Mannheim use a dialect form of the name Pfalz without the "f", pronouncing it "Paltz." Records of the New Paltz [[Reformed Church]], which was formed in 1683, show the name of the settlement was first expressed not in German, nor in English, but in French: ''Nouveau Palatinat''.{{Citation needed|date=September 2008}} The community was governed by a kind of corporation called the ''Duzine'', referring to the 12 partners who acquired the royal patent. That form of government continued well past the time of the [[American Revolution]], by special action of the [[New York State]] [[legislature]].

The {{convert|40000|acre}} or so of the patent, stretching to the [[Hudson River]] and augmented soon by the other patents on the south, were eventually divided among those twelve partners, their relatives, and a few friends into large plots – part wilderness and part farm. The farms were grouped principally around the heights west and east of the [[Wallkill River]]. The commercial center serving the agricultural base was located on the east shore of the Wallkill River, in the area where the first settlers had built their shelters. The street is now known as [[Huguenot Street Historic District|Huguenot Street]].

[[Image:Huguenot houses in New Paltz.jpg|thumb|left|Stone houses of [[Huguenot Street Historic District|Historic Huguenot Street]] in New Paltz. They are among the surviving examples of early stone houses built by Europeans in North America.]] There, the church, schools, [[blacksmith]], [[seamstress]]es, and stores flourished for the benefit of farmers who required goods such as seed, tools, clothing, and food not available on all farms, including [[alcoholic beverages]]. The church, which was also used as a school, was located here. Many of the buildings still stand today, as a living museum community.

Population slowly spread from the Wallkill up along the street now known as North Front Street and then along what is now Chestnut Street. In the 19th century, development continued along what is now Main Street. The secession of the town of [[Lloyd, New York|Lloyd]] and parts of [[Shawangunk, New York|Shawangunk]], [[Esopus, New York|Esopus]], and [[Gardiner (town), New York|Gardiner]], between 1843 and 1853, reduced New Paltz to its present size. In 1887, the village of New Paltz was incorporated within the eponymous town.

Higher education has been one of the main concerns of the community since the 1830s, with facilities on Huguenot and North Front streets. Late in the nineteenth century, the college was built in the area of Plattekill Avenue and Manheim Boulevard, where the [[State University of New York at New Paltz]] now stands.

The [[Wallkill Valley Railroad]] reached New Paltz by 1870, and provided passenger service through the town until 1937. After the rail line's closure in 1977, the section of the corridor running through New Paltz was converted to the [[Wallkill Valley Rail Trail]], and the former [[train station]] in New Paltz was renovated as a restaurant, the [[New Paltz station|Station]].
==Geography==
According to the [[United States Census Bureau]], the village has a total area of {{convert|1.8|mi2|km2}}, of which {{convert|1.7|mi2|km2}}  is land and {{convert|0.04|mi2|km2}} (1.70%) is water.

The [[Wallkill River]] runs north along the western border of New Paltz, flowing into the Rondout Creek and eventually the [[Hudson River]].

As of the [[census]] of 2000,<ref name="GR2">{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=January 31, 2008|title=U.S. Census website}}</ref> there were 6,034 people, 1898 households, and 586 families residing in the village. The [[population density]] was {{convert|3482.5|/mi2|/km2|disp=preunit|people |people}}. There were 1,957 housing units at an average density of {{convert|1,129.5|/mi2|/km2}}. The racial makeup of the village was 73.42% [[White (U.S. Census)|white]], 7.79% [[African American (U.S. Census)|black]] or [[Race (United States Census)|African American]], 0.27% [[Native Americans of the United States|Native American]], 7.01% [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 0.10% [[Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)|Pacific Islander]], 8.35% from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 3.07% from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race were 11.93% of the population.

There were 1,898 households, out of which 12.9% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 21.1% were [[Marriage|married couples]] living together, 7.3% had a female householder with no husband present, and 69.1% were non-families. 41.1% of all households were made up of individuals, and 7.2% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.03 and the average family size was 2.66.

In the village, the age of population was disbursed as such: 6.9% under the age of 18, 58.7% from 18 to 24, 19.0% from 25 to 44, 10.1% from 45 to 64, and 5.3% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 22 years. For every 100 females, there were 80.8 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 78.8 males.

The median income for a household in the village was $21,747, and the median income for a family was $51,186. Males had a median income of $33,103 versus $22,935 for females. The [[per capita income]] for the village was $11,644. About 11.8% of families and 36.9% of the population were below the [[poverty line]], including 18.6% of those under age 18 and 12.2% of those age 65 or over.
== Politics ==
The mayor is Alexandria Wojcik, who assumed the role in an acting capacity on January 1, 2026, after former mayor Tim Rogers was elected as the supervisor of the town of [[New Paltz (town), New York|New Paltz]]. She was formally appointed by the board on February 18, 2026, making her the first openly [[LGBTQ people|LGBTQ]] mayor of New Paltz and the first woman to hold the office since 1983.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Kemble |first=William J. |date=2026-02-19|title=New Paltz appoints Wojcik as village mayor|url=https://www.dailyfreeman.com/2026/02/19/new-paltz-appoints-wojcik-as-village-mayor/|access-date=2026-02-20|website=Daily Freeman|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Ward |first=Terrence P. |date=February 23, 2026 |url=https://hudsonvalleyone.com/2026/02/22/first-woman-appointed-mayor-of-new-paltz-this-century/ |title=First woman appointed mayor of New Paltz this century |website=Hudson Valley One}}</ref> Wojcik is a member of the [[Forward Party (United States)|New York Forward Party]], making her the second third-party Mayor in the Village's history.

The board of trustees meets on the second and fourth Wednesdays of the month at 7:00 p.m. at the village hall. Sewer and water districts for the village are maintained through a department of public works. Rehabilitation of the sewer system, which has been found to overflow raw sewage onto local streets and into the [[Wallkill River|Wallkill]], is expected under a consent order agreed to in 2003.<ref name="mccarthy">{{cite web |last1=McCarthy |first1=Justin |title=New Paltz Prepares Pipe Plans |url=https://oracle.newpaltz.edu/new-paltz-prepares-pipe-plans/ |website=New Paltz Oracle |publisher=SUNY New Paltz |access-date=May 29, 2020 |date=October 21, 2010}}</ref>
=== Activism ===
[[Image:Women in Black in New Paltz, NY.JPG|thumb|Women in Black staging a protest in front of [[Elting Memorial Library]]|right]]The [[Women in Black]] have a small-but-active chapter in New Paltz that has been protesting in front of [[Elting Memorial Library]] weekly since November 2001.<ref name="lubinski">{{cite web|url=http://www.newpaltz.edu/oracle/article.cfm?id=3126|title=New Paltz Women in Black Going on Six Years Strong|last=Lubinski|first=Amy|date=September 6, 2007|work=The New Paltz Oracle|publisher=SUNY New Paltz|access-date=November 28, 2008}}</ref> In 2024, over 200 activists rallied at the library to demonstrate their "outrage" over the [[State University of New York at New Paltz#Student activism|arrest]] of over 100 students at SUNY New Paltz who had created a [[2024 pro-Palestinian protests on university campuses|Gaza solidarity encampment]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://connecticut.news12.com/protesters-voice-outrage-over-handling-of-student-encampment-at-suny-new-paltz |title= Protesters voice outrage over handling of student encampment at SUNY New Paltz |last=News 12 Staff|first=|date=May 4, 2024 |website=[[News 12 Networks|News 12 Connecticut]] |access-date=May 6, 2024}}</ref>
=== Electoral history ===
Village mayoral elections are held every four years, with the mayor serving a four-year term. Prior to 2015, elections were traditionally nonpartisan, with candidates sometimes running on informal or locally created party lines rather than major-party ballots. 

Thomas Nyquist was elected mayor in 1987 and served four consecutive four-year terms, before being defeated in 2003 after sixteen years in office, one of the longest mayoral tenures in the village's history.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-12-09 |title=Thomas Nyquist - Hudson Valley One |url=https://hudsonvalleyone.com/obituaries/thomas-nyquist/ |access-date=2026-07-24 |language=en-US}}</ref> 

In 2003, 26-year-old political activist Jason West won the mayoral election in a three-way race, taking office alongside two other candidates associated with the Green Party (Rebecca Rotzler and Julia Walsh).<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sullivan |first=Robert |date=2004-03-28 |title=Mayor With A Mission |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/03/28/magazine/mayor-with-a-mission.html |access-date=2026-07-24 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> West gained international attention as part of the first [[Green Party of the United States|Green Party]] majority elected in New York State, and later for risking criminal prosecution to marry 25 same-sex couples.<ref name="SF Chronicle">{{cite web|url=https://www.sfgate.com/news/article/N-Y-village-mayor-jumps-into-same-sex-marriage-2816347.php|title=N.Y. village mayor jumps into same-sex marriage fray|date=February 28, 2004|access-date=September 15, 2008|first=Justin|last=Silverman|work=San Francisco Chronicle}}</ref> He lost his reelection bid on May 1, 2007, to village trustee Terry Dungan.

Dungan did not seek reelection in 2011, announcing he would instead focus on recovering from a stroke he had suffered on Christmas Day.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Alter |first=Maxim |date=2011-03-10 |title=Dungan Not Running for Mayor |url=https://oracle.newpaltz.edu/dungan-not-running-for-mayor/ |access-date=2026-07-24 |website=The New Paltz Oracle |language=en-US}}</ref> West returned to the race that year, running on the "Cooperative Party" ticket, and won a second non-consecutive term. West scored 381 votes in that contest.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wilder |first=Kimberly |date=May 4, 2011 |title=Jason West wins for Mayor in New Paltz |url=https://independentpoliticalreport.com/2011/05/jason-west-wins-for-mayor-in-new-paltz/ |access-date=2026-07-24 |website=Independent Political Report}}</ref>

In 2015, Tim Rogers won the mayoral race with 353 votes, defeating incumbent Jason West (204 votes), village trustee Sally Rhoads (177 votes), and Amy Cohen (137 votes) — a four-way race that drew roughly 870 total ballots.<ref>{{Cite web |last=VillageClerk |date=2015-05-06 |title=2015 Election Results • Village of New Paltz |url=https://www.villageofnewpaltz.gov/2015-election-results/ |access-date=2026-07-24 |website=Village of New Paltz |language=en-US}}</ref> Rogers ran unopposed in 2019, receiving 364 votes, and again ran unopposed in 2023, backed by both the Democratic and [[Working Families Party|Working Families]] parties.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ward |first=Terence P. |date=2019-05-08 |title=Newcomers Wojcik and Zipp win New Paltz Village Board seats - Hudson Valley One |url=https://hudsonvalleyone.com/2019/05/08/newcomers-wojcik-and-zipp-win-new-paltz-village-board-seats/ |access-date=2026-07-24 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Clayton |first=Emily |date=2023-11-08 |title=New Paltz and Ulster County General Election 2023 Results |url=https://oracle.newpaltz.edu/ulster-county-election-results/ |access-date=2026-07-24 |website=The New Paltz Oracle |language=en-US}}</ref> 

Rogers vacated the mayoralty when he won election as [[New Paltz (town), New York|Town]] Supervisor in November 2025, defeating incumbent Amanda Gotto with 75.95% of the vote.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Kelly |first1=Patrick |last2=Jones |first2=Cyrus |date=2025-11-05 |title=Results are in: Rogers Victorious in Town Supervisor Race |url=https://oracle.newpaltz.edu/2025-election-results/ |access-date=2026-07-24 |website=The New Paltz Oracle |language=en-US}}</ref> Deputy Mayor Alexandria Wojcik became acting mayor as Rogers assumed his new role and was formally appointed by the board on February 18, 2026.<ref name=":0" /> Wojcik had originally been elected to the village board as a trustee after running on a self-styled "[[Do it yourself|D.I.Y. — Do It Yourself]]" party line with a $0 campaign in 2019. On November 3, 2026, Wojcik was elected to position with over 90% of the vote running unopposed.<ref name="app.enhancedvoting.com-1">{{Cite web |title=Election Results |url=https://app.enhancedvoting.com/results/public/ulster-county-ny/elections/GE2026_20261019155937 |access-date=2026-11-04 |website=app.enhancedvoting.com}}</ref>  

On November 3, 2026, residents in both the Town and Village of New Paltz voted against consolidation, with Town residents voting 64/35% against and Village residents voting 59/40%<ref name="app.enhancedvoting.com-1" />

== Media ==
=== Newspapers ===
[[Image:Charles J. Ackert.png|thumb|left|Charles J. Ackert, the first newspaper publisher in New Paltz]]
The first local newspaper in New Paltz, the ''New Paltz Times'', was founded by Charles J. Ackert, who printed its first issue on July 6, 1860. It was a weekly paper in which the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] was supported. The ''New Paltz Independent'', a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] newspaper, was founded in 1868.<ref>{{Harvnb|Sylvester|1880|p=14}}</ref> Both the ''Times'' and ''Independent'' merged in 1919,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.huguenotstreet.org/library_archives/exhibits_research/temperance.php |title=The Temperance Movement New Paltz during the Late Nineteenth Century: A Research Guide |first=Mary |last=Dew |publisher=[[Huguenot Street Historic District]] |date=Fall 2002 |access-date=January 2, 2011}}</ref> becoming the ''New Paltz Independent and Times'' that ran until 1972, when it became the ''Old Dutch New Paltz Independent and Times''. That same year it was renamed the ''Old Dutch independent'', and ran until it was discontinued in 1975. The ''New Paltz News'' was founded in 1935, and merged with the [[Wallkill, Ulster County, New York|Wallkill]] paper ''Wallkill Valley World'' in 1980. The ''Huguenot Herald'' was first published in 1976 and merged in 1985 with the [[Highland, Ulster County, New York|Highland]] paper, the ''Highland Herald''.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nysl.nysed.gov/nysnp/all/456.htm |title=Ulster County (NY) newspapers on microfilm and paper at all NYS locations |publisher=[[New York State Library]] |access-date=January 14, 2011}}</ref> At SUNY New Paltz, a college newspaper, the ''New Paltz Oracle'', was founded in 1938.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.newpaltz.edu/oracle/article.cfm?id=3645 |title=Student Senate debates over The New Paltz Oracle, amends Bylaws Regarding Line-Item Budget Requests |date=March 27, 2008 |access-date=January 31, 2011 |publisher=[[State University of New York at New Paltz|SUNY New Paltz]] |newspaper=New Paltz Oracle |volume=17 |issue=79 |first=Amy |last=Lubinski}}</ref> The ''Huguenot Herald'' and ''New Paltz News'' continued to run until they were merged by the owner of Ulster Publishing as the ''New Paltz Times''<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.townoflloyd.com/pdf/highlandandnewspapers.pdf |title=Highland and its newspapers: Post Pioneer-New Paltz Times merger brings end to 121 years of intensely local journalism |first=Ethan P. |last=Jackman |newspaper=Highland Mid-Hudson Post |location=Highland, NY |date=November 13, 2008 |access-date=January 14, 2011 }}</ref> in 2001.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nysl.nysed.gov/nysnp/156.htm |title=Ulster County (NY) newspapers on microfilm at NYSL |publisher=[[New York State Library]] |access-date=January 31, 2011}}</ref> The modern ''New Paltz Times'', which had no continuity with the 19th-century paper of the same name, was published weekly until 2020, when it was merged into ''Hudson Valley One''.
==Culture==
[[File:Newpaltz03-2017.jpg|thumb|Lower Main Street, New Paltz|right]] 
New Paltz hosts a number of cultural events.
===Unity in Diversity Day===
This event, paid for through the village, town, and SUNY New Paltz, celebrated the differences among people through food, spoken word poetry, artistic endeavors and theatrical performance. The last known theme, in 2007, was derived from [[Dr. Seuss]]'s story about [[Sneetch]]es.
===Halloween===
;Haunted Hasbrouck Park
For over a quarter of a century the Guenther family put on a free [[Haunted attraction (simulated)|haunted house]] for area residents, which attracted thousands of visitors on [[Halloween]] night. After complaints about traffic and noise concerns, owners Ann and Dan Guenther announced in 2006 that they would no longer create the attraction. However, interest continued, and the attraction was relocated to Hasbrouck Park in 2007,<ref name="nptimes1007">{{cite news |first=Erin |last=Quinn |title=Fright Fest: Haunted House moves from Center Street to Hasbrouck Park |url= http://www.ulsterpublishing.com/index.cfm?fuseaction=article&articleID=426391 |work=New Paltz Times |publisher=Ulster Publishing |date=October 11, 2007 |access-date=October 11, 2007 }}</ref> utilizing the park's castle [[playground]] as a centerpiece. This move also increased community involvement for the event for the two years it was held there, drawing upon the local YMCA, village employees, and volunteers from the area.<ref name="nptimes1008">{{cite news |first=Erin |last=Quinn |title=Oh the horror: Haunted house returns to Hasbrouck Park |url= http://www.ulsterpublishing.com/index.cfm?fuseaction=article&articleID=426391 |work=New Paltz Times |publisher=Ulster Publishing |date=October 16, 2008 |access-date=October 18, 2008 }}</ref>

;Halloween parade
A parade on Halloween night has been conducted through the village since the 1960s. It begins at the New Paltz middle school and ends at [[Huguenot Street Historic District|Historic Huguenot Street]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Paltz Halloween Parade |url=https://www.hudsonvalleysojourner.com/free-events/new-paltz-halloween-parade/ |access-date=2026-11-03 |website=Hudson Valley Sojourner |language=en-US}}</ref>

;Haunted Huguenot Street
On the nights leading up to Halloween, stories of spirits, tragedy, misfortune and the paranormal fill the 330-year-old street under the moniker of "Haunted Huguenot Street" tours.

;Night of 100 Pumpkins
Since 1990 this pumpkin-carving contest has been hosted at a local eatery called the Bakery.<ref>[http://www.ulsterpublishing.com/index.cfm?fuseaction=article&articleID=320553 Halloween Happenings] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080607194642/http://www.ulsterpublishing.com/index.cfm?fuseaction=article&articleID=320553 |date=June 7, 2008 }}, New Paltz Times, October 2004, accessed October 27, 2007, at 13:08</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ilovethebakery.com/halloween_fun.htm |title=The Bakery's Night of 100 Pumpkins Page |access-date=December 1, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070811005250/http://www.ilovethebakery.com/halloween_fun.htm |archive-date=August 11, 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
===Pride march===
A pride march celebrating [[LGBTQ culture|LGBT culture]] is a focus of pride celebrations in June, drawing a number of out-of-town visitors to see the community where same-sex weddings were performed when they were still illegal.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ward |first=Terence P. |date=2025-06-02 |title=Thousands take to streets for 20th annual New Paltz pride march and festival (photos) - Hudson Valley One |url=https://hudsonvalleyone.com/2025/06/02/thousands-take-to-streets-for-20th-annual-new-paltz-pride-march-and-festival-photos/ |access-date=2025-06-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>
===Memorial Day parade===
The local Memorial Day parade is always held on the actual Memorial Day, not the Monday substitute agreed upon in Congress.
===Turkey Trot===
A fundraising run on Thanksgiving to support Family of New Paltz.
===New Paltz Regatta===
A river race using home made boats that was started in 1955 by [[Delta Kappa]] fraternity at [[SUNY New Paltz]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.newpaltzregatta.com/index.php?id=history|title=History - New Paltz Regatta|publisher=NewPaltzRegatta.com}}</ref>  It has since been taken over by local citizens and is held every year to celebrate the start of summer.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dailyfreeman.com/arts-and-entertainment/20170503/new-paltz-regatta-homemade-boats-to-race-down-wallkill-river-on-may-7|title=New Paltz Regatta|last=Hubert|first=Brian|date=May 3, 2017|publisher=DailyFreeman.com}}</ref>
=== New Paltz in fiction ===
*New Paltz was the place in which the character Penny Johnson ([[Cynthia Rhodes]]) got an [[abortion]] in the 1987 movie ''[[Dirty Dancing]]'', which was set in the early 1960s.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.recordonline.com/article/20040530/News/305309990|title=Local references in movies and television|author=<!-- Staff -->|work=[[Times-Herald Record]]|date=December 16, 2010|access-date=January 2, 2015}}</ref>
*It was also the village visited by Miss Sara Howard during the investigation of a sadistic killer's origins, in the novel ''[[The Alienist]]'' by [[Caleb Carr]].
*The town is mentioned in [[Paul Simon]]'s song "Killer Wants to Go to College" on his album ''[[Songs from The Capeman]]''.
*New Paltz was fictionalized as "Little Heart" in the 2013 novel ''The Cusp of Sad'' by Nikki Pison about the 1980s punk rock street and music scene.
==Recreation==
=== Biking and hiking ===
The Mohonk Preserve, Mohonk Mountain House and Minnewaska State Park offer biking and hiking opportunities in an area deemed picturesque by tourism supporters.

The [[Wallkill Valley Rail Trail]] passes through New Paltz and runs concurrently with the [[Empire State Trail]] for a distance.

The River-to-Ridge trail runs from the village line into the Mohonk Preserve.
==Transportation==
===Automobile===
New Paltz is exit 18 on the [[New York State Thruway]], which is also designated as [[Interstate 87 (New York)|Interstate 87]].
===Bus===
There is frequent bus service between The [[Port Authority Bus Terminal]] in New York City and New Paltz provided by [[Trailways of New York]], with connections to many other villages and cities in New York State. Express bus service is also available from New Paltz to New York City via Trailways of New York, serving the park-ride lot at Exit 18 of the Thruway. [[Ulster County Area Transit]] also provides service to [[Metro-North Railroad]] in [[Poughkeepsie (city), New York|Poughkeepsie]], along with local bus service to [[Kingston, New York|Kingston]], [[Newburgh (town), New York|Newburgh]], and points in between along Route 32. In January 2009 the New Paltz Loop Bus, stopping at points throughout the community, was launched.
===Air===
[[Stewart International Airport]] is the nearest major airport to New Paltz. It is located in Newburgh, thirty minutes to the south.
===Rail=== 
[[File:New Paltz station postcard.jpg|thumb|left|The former New York Central station]]
[[File:New Paltz Train Station.jpg|thumb|right|The former station, [[New Paltz station|La Stazione]], as viewed from the [[Wallkill Valley Rail Trail]]]]
The [[Wallkill Valley Railroad]], founded in 1866, stretched from Montgomery to Kingston. The New Paltz railroad station was originally built in 1870,<ref>{{Cite news |newspaper=New Paltz Times |date=September 1, 1870 |location=New Paltz, NY}}</ref> rebuilt after a 1907 fire.<ref>{{Cite news |newspaper=New Paltz Independent |date=December 31, 1907 |location=New Paltz, NY}}</ref> The railroad and station later came under [[New York Central Railroad|New York Central]] ownership. The NYC operated two trains a day, each direction, on a Kingston-New Paltz-Montgomery run. At Kingston, connections were available trains north to Albany and south to Weehawken, New Jersey.<ref>{{cite journal |title=New York Central Railroad, Tables 80 and 82-Walkill Valley Branch |journal=Official Guide of the Railways |publisher=National Railway Publication Company |volume=64 |issue=9|date=February 1932}}</ref> The passenger service through New Paltz ended in 1937, and the rail division was abandoned by [[Conrail]] in 1983. The former roadbed was converted for use as the [[Wallkill Valley Rail Trail]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.gorailtrail.org/ |title=Wallkill Valley Rail Trail site |access-date=December 10, 2004 |archive-date=August 17, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070817064921/http://www.gorailtrail.org/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The former station (now called [[New Paltz station|La Stazione]]) was sold to private interests in 1959.<ref>{{Cite news |newspaper=New Paltz News |location=New Paltz, NY |date=April 13, 1977 |title='No Bar in R.R. Station', Zoning Bd. Of Appeals}}</ref> The building was in a state of disrepair by the early 1980s,<ref>{{Cite news |first=Jeff |last=Muise |page=30 |newspaper=[[Times Herald-Record]] |publisher=[[Dow Jones Local Media Group]] |date=January 25, 1984 |location=Middletown, NY}}</ref> but renovated in 1988<ref>{{Cite news |title=New Paltz rail station to become real estate office |newspaper=Huguenot Herald |date=January 7, 1988}}</ref> and converted to an Italian restaurant in 1999.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Pasta junction – on the right track in New Paltz |page=24 |newspaper=[[Times Herald-Record]] |publisher=[[Dow Jones Local Media Group]] |date=July 2, 1999 |location=Middletown, NY}}</ref>

The nearest active railroad station is the [[Poughkeepsie (Metro-North station)|Poughkeepsie Metro-North station]], which is served by several [[Amtrak]] trains and is the terminus for the [[Metro-North Railroad]]'s Hudson Line. The Hudson Line stretches from Poughkeepsie to [[Grand Central Terminal]] in [[New York City]]. Poughkeepsie is a 15-20 minute drive east of New Paltz.
===Transportation plan===
In 2006, the town and village officials agreed to pay for a transportation study to analyze the transportation needs of the area. The study's suggestions included turning Main Street into a one-way route and improving bicycle and pedestrian access. An implementation committee was appointed in 2007 to study ways to use the plan.
